newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin tells NATO - don't play Russian roulette.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin tells NATO - don't play Russian roulette.

text.p: The Kremlin hailed its security deal with NATO as a diplomatic triumph on Thursday, but warned the Western alliance that offering membership to former Soviet republics would be like playing Russian roulette.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said NATO would put the accord, to be signed in Paris on Tuesday, and its entire relationship with Russia at risk if it tried to draw in the former outposts of the Soviet Union.

"We hope that sensible leaders in the West will not want to play Russian roulette," Yastrzhembsky told a round table discussion, referring to the daredevil game in which gamblers put one bullet in a six-shot revolver, spin the chamber, put the gun to their heads and fire.

"Expanding the bloc at some time in the future to bring in former Soviet republics would force Russia to review its whole set of legal relations with the West, including the Founding Act which will be signed in Paris, and to review its foreign policy priorities."
He gave no further details but specifically objected to NATO membership for the Baltic states -- Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia.
Lithuanian membership could mean the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, which borders Lithuania and Poland, was completely cut off by NATO members.
Moscow and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation agreed terms for the accord last week, hoping to lay the foundations of the former Cold War foes' relations into the next century.

The agreement is also designed to address Russian concerns over NATO's plans to offer membership to at least three countries from the former Soviet bloc in July. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join.
"The supreme aim, the aim of preserving trust between Russia and the West, between Russia and the NATO states, was like a lode star, so to say, for the participants in the talks," Yastrzhembsky said.
"It was possible, by keeping to this aim, to reach a reasonable and balanced document."

Yastrzhembsky, who also coordinates foreign policy in the Kremlin, acknowledged that the agreement, creating a joint Russia-NATO council on some security matters, was open to different interpretations.

He said much work had to be done to ensure that the accord, which Russia says gives it binding guarantees against NATO basing nuclear weapons and building up forces in new member states, is carried out to the letter.
But he said no drama should be made out of this.
His comments were part of a Kremlin campaign to explain the document to the Russian public and counter the communists and nationalists who say Yeltsin has sold out Russia's national interests.
Most participants of the "round table" supported the deal but one expert said Moscow should not have signed it.
Andranik Migranyan, a member of the loose advisory Presidential Council, made clear he believed signing the document implied Russian acceptance of NATO expansion.

"I categorically oppose the line of confrontation with NATO. Confrontation with NATO would really be suicide," he said. "But I do not think that not signing the agreement with NATO means automatically taking the line of confrontation with NATO."
The Kremlin says it does not imply this and continues to criticise the Western defence alliance's enlargement.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is due to continue the Kremlin's efforts to explain and justify the agreement with NATO by addressing a closed session of parliament on Friday.
